profiles.meeting_scenario: An acute care surgery planning huddle is held mid-morning for a 64-year-old woman admitted overnight with acute calculous cholecystitis, leukocytosis, and a bilirubin that rose to 2.2 mg/dL yesterday but is lower this morning after antibiotics and fluids; she also has obesity and a prior lower abdominal surgery, so the team wants to confirm the operative plan for an add-on laparoscopic cholecystectomy with possible intraoperative cholangiogram and possible transcystic duct work if needed. The agenda is to align on timing for the add-on case, preoperative antibiotic and imaging assumptions, OR setup needs if biliary anatomy is unclear, and the expected postoperative pathway. The expected outcome is a shared plan for the afternoon case, including what orders and logistics the PA will handle and what contingencies the surgeon expects intraoperatively.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.expertise: Emergency general surgery, laparoscopic biliary surgery, intraoperative cholangiography, difficult gallbladder decision-making
members.background: Board-certified general surgeon who leads the hospital's acute care surgery service and regularly performs urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomies for complicated gallbladder disease.
members.private_state: She wants to get the patient to the OR this afternoon before the case becomes a late-night add-on, avoid unnecessary delays or extra resource bookings, and preserve flexibility to decide intraoperatively whether a cholangiogram is actually needed.
hidden_assumptions: A patient already receiving therapeutic ceftriaxone and metronidazole is generally 'covered' for the trip to the OR unless the timing becomes clearly off-schedule.

Saying to 'have cholangiogram available' means the team should be able to obtain fluoroscopy and the IOC tray if she asks for it, not that those resources must be physically in the room from incision.
If bilirubin and symptoms are improving, an outside MRCP report without a filling defect is adequate background information even if the actual images are not yet in PACS.

When she says the patient will 'probably go home tomorrow,' she means discharge is likely once pain is controlled, the patient is tolerating diet, and there is no operative complication, even if morning labs are not fully normalized.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: Inpatient perioperative coordination, pre-op orders, postoperative pathway management, discharge planning for emergency general surgery patients
members.background: An experienced PA who manages the acute care surgery floor list, prepares add-on cholecystectomy patients for the OR, and translates attending plans into orders, handoffs, and discharge milestones.
members.private_state: She wants the case to run smoothly without last-minute scrambling, avoid being blamed for preventable OR delays, and set up a postoperative plan that will not surprise the floor team tomorrow morning.
hidden_assumptions: If the attending says the patient is 'covered' on antibiotics, no separate pre-incision prophylaxis reminder or clarification is needed because the current regimen already satisfies what the OR will expect.

If a surgeon mentions a possible cholangiogram during planning, the safest interpretation is that fluoroscopy access and the cholangiogram supplies should be arranged from the start of the case rather than fetched later.

When an attending says the patient will 'go home tomorrow,' that usually implies the standard morning discharge checklist on this service, including repeat CBC/CMP/LFTs that are reassuring enough for sign-out.
If the surgeon casually refers to 'the MRCP,' that implies the imaging itself is effectively available to the team, not merely an outside dictated report scanned into the chart.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the patient to be 'covered' on antibiotics
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the patient is 'covered' on ceftriaxone and metronidazole until the OR.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Park means the patient is being appropriately treated for cholecystitis right now, and unless the timing drifts substantially, she does not view antibiotic timing as a separate planning item worth discussing in detail.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya means no additional peri-incision antibiotic task, reminder, or clarification needs to be built into the pre-op plan because 'covered' already settles the OR-facing antibiotic question.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Patients with acute cholecystitis are commonly already on antibiotics, so the phrase feels complete and routine; both hear it as reassuring shorthand and neither expects the other to be using a slightly different operational meaning.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to have cholangiogram available if the duct still looks questionable.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Park means she wants the option to request an IOC if anatomy is unclear or the duct seems suspicious, but she expects a standard lap chole setup at start and assumes fluoroscopy can be pulled in only if needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya means the C-arm, cholangiogram catheter tray, and related support should be arranged proactively from case start because 'available' in an add-on room means physically ready before the incision.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are trying to avoid delays and both use the same cooperative phrase, but they silently optimize for different failure modes: the surgeon for over-preparation and the PA for mid-case scrambling.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the patient will likely be 'home tomorrow' if the case is straightforward.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Park means a next-day discharge is appropriate as long as the patient is clinically well after surgery, with pain controlled and oral intake tolerated, even if liver tests are still mildly abnormal but trending in the right direction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya means the patient is on the usual postoperative day-1 discharge pathway, which in practice includes repeat morning labs and enough numerical improvement to make the floor team comfortable sending her out.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Next-day discharge after laparoscopic cholecystectomy is common enough that the phrase sounds unambiguous; the underlying threshold for what proves readiness is rarely unpacked unless a problem later emerges.

misalignment_points.topic: What is meant by 'the MRCP was negative'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the MRCP was negative and the bilirubin is coming down.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Park is relying on the outside-hospital dictated MRCP report and the morning lab trend, and she assumes that is sufficient context for proceeding without chasing the actual image set before surgery.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Priya assumes that when Dr. Park references 'the MRCP,' the actual study is effectively available in the system or otherwise accessible if someone needs to review it later that day.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The chart contains enough documentation for both people to talk naturally about 'the MRCP' as a shared object, so neither notices that one is thinking of a written report and the other of accessible imaging.
